Fisheries and Oceans Canada.</ref> is a species of [[seaweed]] in the family [[Codiaceae]]. It originates in the [[Pacific Ocean]] near Japan and has become an [[invasive species]] on the coasts of the Northern [[Atlantic Ocean]].

==Description==
[[File:Dead Man's Fingers (Codium fragile) - Tor Bay Provincial Park, Nova Scotia 2022-07-27 (02).jpg|thumb|From [[Nova Scotia]]]]
This siphonous [[green algae|green alga]] is of two subspecies in [[Ireland]] and [[Great Britain]]. They are similar, both are dark green in color. It forms long erect finger-like fronds. These grow to 40 cm or more long branching dichotomously. The cortex of the branches is formed by closely packed utricles, these are small cylindrical club-shaped structures formed from a single cell up to 1200 μm ([[micrometre]]s) long.<ref name="Burrows">Burrows, E.M. 1991. ''Seaweeds of the British Isles''. Natural History Museum, London {{ISBN|0-565-00981-8}}</ref> The rounded tips of these closely packed utricles give the frond a velvety texture.<ref>Dickinson, C.I. 1963 ''British Seaweeds''. The Kew Series, Eyre & Spottiswoode</ref> The fronds hang down from rocks during low tide, hence the nickname "dead man's fingers".<ref>[http://www.mbari.org/staff/conn/botany/greens/kathy/index.htm ''Codium fragile'': Dead Man's Fingers.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516162542/http://www.mbari.org/staff/conn/botany/greens/kathy/index.htm |date=16 May 2011 }} Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute. 1996.</ref> The "fingers" are branches up to a centimeter wide and sometimes over 30 centimeters long.

''Codium fragile'' occurs in the low [[intertidal zone]], and subtidal on high-energy beaches.

It has no [[gametophyte]] stage, and male and female gametes are both produced on separate plants.

==Subspecies==
Subspecies of ''C. fragile'' can only be distinguished microscopically.

===''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''atlanticum''===
This subspecies can be distinguished by the mucron or tip of the utricles. In this subspecies the mucron is short, no more than 20 μm long.<ref name="Burrows"/>

The first European record of ''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''atlanticum'' is known to have arrived in the southwest of [[Ireland]] around 1808. From there it may have spread by rafting or floating in the sea. Approximately 30 years later, it was found in [[Scotland]]. It is thought to have originally come from the [[Pacific Ocean]] near [[Japan]].

Since 1840, when it was first discovered in Scotland, it has spread the entire length of Britain, including [[Shetland]]. Between 1949 and 1955 it is known to have spread between [[Berwick-upon-Tweed]] and [[St. Andrews]], [[Fife]], a distance of 80 km. Populations of this algae occur mostly in northern Britain. Elsewhere in Europe it is found in several places, including Norway, Netherlands, France, Spain and the [[Azores]].

This species displaces the native ''[[Codium tomentosum]]''.

''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''atlanticum'' is used as food in the [[Far East]].<ref name=jncc>[http://jncc.defra.gov.uk/page-1678 ''Codium fragile'' ssp. ''atlanticum''.] Joint Nature Conservation Committee, UK.</ref>
[[File:Codium fragile (Suringar) Hariot, 1889.jpg|thumb|right|Close-up]]

===''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''tomentosoides''===
This subspecies is distinguished from ''C.fragile'' subsp. ''atlanticum'' by its very pointed mucron (the tip of the utricle) – up to μm 68 long.<ref name="Burrows"/>

The subspecies ''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''tomentosoides''<ref>[http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?fr=1&si=796&sts ''Codium fragile'' ssp. ''tomentosoides''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304060902/http://www.issg.org/database/species/ecology.asp?fr=1&si=796&sts |date=4 March 2016 }} Global Invasive Species Database. ISSG.</ref><ref>[http://massbay.mit.edu/exoticspecies/exoticmaps/descriptions_intro.html ''Codium fragile'' ssp. ''tomentosoides''.] Introduced Species: Descriptions. MIT Sea Grant.</ref> (syn. ''Codium mucronatum'' var. ''tomentosoides''), occurs along nearly the whole coastline of the eastern [[United States]], from the [[Gulf of St. Lawrence]] in Canada to [[North Carolina]]. It is a rapidly spreading invasive species.<ref name=wsu/> It originated in the [[Pacific Ocean]] around Japan, and was introduced into [[New York (state)|New York]] from [[Europe]] in 1957. Its presence was first recorded in 1964 in the [[Gulf of Maine]] at [[Boothbay, Maine|Boothbay]]. It is now recorded around [[Ireland]].<ref>Morton, O. 2003. The marine macroalgae of County Donegal, Ireland. ''Bulletin of Ireland biogeography Society'' No 27: 3 – 164</ref> It has also been recorded from the [[Scilly Isles]], the [[Channel Islands]], and the south and west coasts of [[England]] and [[Scotland]].<ref name="Burrows"/>

This is a dominant subspecies in the subtidal zone, attaching to almost any hard surface. This results in increased maintenance labor for [[aquaculture|aquaculturists]] and reduces the productivity of cultured marine life. In established [[shellfish]] beds, this species can become a nuisance; it may attach to shellfish and then float away, carrying the animals with it. This was the inspiration for the common name "oyster thief".<ref name=ca/>

===''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''scandinavicum''===
This subspecies was introduced from Asiatic coasts of the Pacific to Norway, and to [[Denmark]] in 1919.<ref name=jncc/>

=== ''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''novae-zelandiae'' ===
[[File:Codium fragile novae-zelandiae 31396862.jpg|thumb|''Codium fragile'' subsp. ''novae-zelandiae'']]
This subspecies is found in the low intertidal to subtidal zones around [[New Zealand]] at the North Island, South Island, Chatham Islands, Stewart Island, Auckland Island, Campbell Island as well as around the [[Falkland Islands]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=New Zealand seaweeds : an illustrated guide|last=W. A.|first=Nelson|publisher=Te Papa Press|year=2013|isbn=9780987668813|location=Wellington, New Zealand|pages=30|oclc=841897290|author-link=Wendy Nelson (marine scientist)}}</ref>
